controls.reason: Deciding whether the documentation states the real problem and correctly identifies the intended users requires semantic product judgment, not just finding named sections.
Whether scope, non-goals, and deferrals are truly explicit and complete for this release depends on contextual interpretation of the product plan.
A complete feature-to-criteria link can be checked, but whether each criterion is genuinely testable and sufficient for its feature requires semantic review.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every feature in the sealed release-scope inventory references at least one acceptance-criteria record.

controls.reason: Ranking journeys by business and user impact is a value judgment; informed reviewers can assign different rankings from the same product evidence.
Which journeys are critical and which listed journey types are applicable depends on the product and its users, so a fixed checker cannot prove completeness.
Links between inventoried dependencies and failure-behavior records are checkable, but adequacy across partial-failure modes and product expectations requires contextual review.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every inventoried critical dependency references a release-bound unavailable-or-partial-failure behavior record.

controls.reason: A condition matrix can be validated structurally, but deciding whether it covers every relevant malformed, incomplete, stale, or conflicting data case requires product judgment.

deterministic_clauses.statement: The release behavior record contains entries for empty, malformed, incomplete, stale, and conflicting data conditions.

controls.reason: Consistency requires interpreting all user-visible language across an open-ended interface and deciding when different terms are acceptable synonyms or real conflicts.
Whether commercial and billing language is unambiguous to users requires semantic and often contractual interpretation; matching field values alone cannot prove clarity.
Records can show that reversal-related behaviors are described, but applicability and the legal or product correctness of cancellation, refund, dispute, and undo behavior need specialist judgment.

deterministic_clauses.statement: The release policy contains version-bound behavior records for each reversal operation declared applicable.

controls.reason: The full set of customer-support obligations comes from commercial promises, contracts, policy, and operating context, so document presence cannot prove completeness.
Alignment among service hours, maintenance, SLOs, SLAs, and contracts requires interpreting obligations and resolving semantic conflicts across authoritative sources.
A release-bound claim inventory and evidence links are checkable, but deciding whether evidence actually substantiates each public claim requires semantic and sometimes legal review.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every inventoried launch claim references current evidence bound to the released artifact or behavior version.

controls.reason: Acceptance of final critical-journey behavior is an accountable product-management decision; a scanner may validate its record but cannot make the acceptance.
Metric, operator, threshold, and window fields can be validated, but choosing criteria that truly represent launch success is a contextual product decision.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Each recorded launch-success criterion names a metric, comparison operator, threshold, observation window, and release scope.

controls.reason: Failure thresholds and rollback trigger fields can be validated, but whether they are sufficient and appropriate for this launch requires accountable risk judgment.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Each launch-failure or rollback criterion names a metric or event, trigger condition, observation window, and release scope.

controls.reason: Selecting adequate adoption, conversion, quality, reliability, support, and safety indicators depends on product scope and risk, not merely on field presence.
The proposed clause verifies a finite period but not that it was defined before launch completion or that completion cannot occur before the required observation semantics are satisfied.
controls.counterexample_analysis: A team declares the launch complete at 10:00, then creates a record at 11:00 with a finite 09:00–09:30 observation period. The clause passes although the period was not defined before completion.

controls.reason: An authority assignment alone does not bind the matrix to this release, prove freshness, or establish that the named identities still hold authority when an action occurs.
controls.counterexample_analysis: A prior-release matrix names an employee whose authority was revoked yesterday. It remains authenticated and assigns all four actions, so the clause passes while the current launch has no valid rollback authority.

controls.reason: Numeric traffic and cohort selectors do not prove that the forecast is current, release-bound, complete across traffic dimensions, or meaningfully represents expected demand.
controls.counterexample_analysis: A stale forecast for the previous release records 100 requests per day and a country selector. It satisfies the clause while the new launch expects 100,000 requests per second from invitation cohorts.

controls.reason: The proposal validates a declared vocabulary value but never compares that declaration with the actual exposure configuration, so it proves documentation rather than whether the launch really has that mode.
controls.counterexample_analysis: The release record says internal while a CDN route makes the release public. The allowed vocabulary check passes although the actual launch is not internal.

controls.reason: Four matching canonical records do not prove that every artifact and person in marketing, sales, support, and operations actually uses those values.
controls.counterexample_analysis: The four official records say 1 September and EU-only, but a sales deck and support script still announce 25 August worldwide. The comparison passes while the functions use conflicting dates and scope.

controls.reason: Release binding and artifact presence are checkable, but determining whether prose, screenshots, pricing, documentation, and legal text semantically match behavior requires human and legal review.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every inventoried launch-content artifact is bound to the assessed release version and has a current content digest.

controls.reason: Delivery records are objectively checkable, but deciding when notification is required depends on contracts, law, migration impact, and changed data-use interpretation.

deterministic_clauses.statement: For every approved notification requirement, an authenticated delivery record identifies the scoped customers, content version, channel, and send time.

controls.reason: The proposal assumes a complete production-service inventory without defining an authoritative boundary or proving that shadow and unmanaged production services cannot be omitted.
controls.counterexample_analysis: A manually deployed production worker is absent from the queried catalog and has no business owner. Every inventoried service maps to an owner, so the anti-join passes while the original every-service claim is false.

controls.reason: The proposed join cannot prove the universal statement until production-service scope and completeness across all control planes are objectively bounded.
controls.counterexample_analysis: A production cron service in a separate account is missing from the inventory and has no engineering owner. All catalogued services have owners, so the proposal passes.

controls.reason: A data catalog is not automatically authoritative for every data set, and the proposal gives no discovery boundary for exports, spreadsheets, replicas, or shadow stores.
controls.counterexample_analysis: A customer export copied into an analyst spreadsheet is absent from the catalog and has no accountable owner. Every catalog row is owned, so the checker passes while an in-scope data set violates the rule.

controls.reason: The check relies on the inventory’s security-sensitivity label, but deciding sensitivity is itself a risk judgment and omitted or misclassified components evade the owner check.
controls.counterexample_analysis: A token-handling component is classified non-sensitive by mistake and has no security contact. The second clause skips it, so both clauses pass despite the real violation.

controls.reason: Release evidence is not a complete authority for every third-party integration and the proposal does not bound browser tags, manual transfers, webhooks, or shadow SaaS use.
controls.counterexample_analysis: A marketing pixel sends production data to a third party but is absent from release evidence and has no owner. Every listed integration is owned, so the proposal passes.

controls.reason: Monitoring and repository sources do not necessarily enumerate dashboards, alerts, and runbooks in SaaS tools, personal spaces, or alternate accounts; completeness is asserted rather than proven.
controls.counterexample_analysis: An active pager alert created directly in a provider console has no owner and is missing from the collected inventory. All inventoried items are owned, so the checker passes.

controls.reason: A scheduler snapshot cannot establish every background process without a sealed definition and inventory across queues, platforms, databases, clients, and external automation.
controls.counterexample_analysis: A database-scheduled cleanup task is not exposed by the queried scheduler and has no owner. Every discovered job maps to an owner, so the proposal passes.

controls.reason: The promise must remain valid across future leave, holidays, and personnel changes; current schedules cannot prove indefinite future coverage and validity.
Provider applicability and the complete provider inventory are not defined, so the checker can omit a required escalation contact while satisfying the fixed contact fields.
controls.counterexample_analysis: The service depends on a payment provider but that provider is absent from the applicability record. Primary, secondary, management, security, and legal contacts exist, so the clauses pass without payment-provider escalation.

controls.reason: Access-change timestamps are checkable, but the word promptly has no threshold in the rule and completeness depends on authoritative personnel and access inventories.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every inventoried offboarding or role-change event has corresponding access-change timestamps for each affected account.

controls.reason: Assigning confidentiality impact requires applying organizational risk appetite and consequence judgment; identical facts can support different accountable classifications.
Assigning integrity impact requires an accountable assessment of consequence and business importance rather than a mechanically discoverable repository fact.
Availability impact classification depends on business-critical journeys, tolerated disruption, and organizational risk criteria requiring accountable judgment.
Privacy impact classification depends on data context, affected people, law, policy, and specialist interpretation that a deterministic checker cannot supply.
Financial and fraud impact depends on business exposure, attacker incentives, limits, and risk appetite, so the impact class is not mechanically determined.
Physical, psychological, societal, and user-safety impacts require domain expertise and ethical or safety judgment beyond bounded technical evidence.
Regulatory and contractual impact can only be classified after interpreting applicable law and agreements by an authorized specialist.
Reputational and customer-trust impact is inherently contextual and depends on stakeholder expectations that fixed evidence cannot authoritatively rank.
Determining which threat actors and accidental sources are likely requires threat intelligence and system-specific judgment; list presence cannot prove likelihood or completeness.
Foreseeable misuse and abuse are open-ended and depend on adversarial imagination and context, so no bounded inventory can prove all foreseeable cases were identified.
The original control requires the existence of a maintained release-specific register, and the proposed authenticated record is bound to the exact release, scope digest, and current revision.

deterministic_clauses.statement: An authenticated risk register exists and is bound to the assessed release identity, scope digest, and current revision.

controls.counterexample_analysis: I tried an empty, stale, or prior-release register: emptiness does not violate this existence-only control, while stale or wrong-release records fail the explicit binding and current-revision checks. No broader risk-quality promise is smuggled into the statement.

controls.reason: Checking fields on existing rows does not establish a complete risk inventory; an empty or selectively incomplete register passes the universal each-risk wording.
controls.counterexample_analysis: The register omits a known supplier-collapse risk but every remaining row has all six required fields. The clause passes although that omitted risk has no owner, likelihood, impact, treatment, evidence, or review date.

controls.reason: The proposal quantifies only over recorded acceptances and has no authoritative inventory of all accepted residual risks, so omitted decisions disappear from evaluation.
controls.counterexample_analysis: Leadership accepts a launch risk in meeting notes but it is never added to the risk register. The recorded-acceptance set is empty, so both clauses pass while the accepted risk and accepter were not recorded.

controls.reason: High-impact applicability, subject-matter expertise, and meaningful independence depend on accountable policy and organizational judgment, while omitted assumptions evade the proposed records.
controls.counterexample_analysis: A critical tax assumption is labeled medium-impact and reviewed by a nominally independent generalist. The policy fields and signed record pass even though no independent tax expert reviewed the truly high-impact assumption.

controls.reason: Whether launch scope remains inside organizational risk appetite is an accountable risk-acceptance determination, not a fact an automated evaluator may decide.
A merely finite expiry does not define the maximum acceptable exception duration, so an exception can remain effectively indefinite while passing both clauses.
controls.counterexample_analysis: An exception receives an expiry in the year 2126 and an active owner. It is finite and not expired today, so the proposal passes despite leaving the exception open for a century.

controls.reason: An executed result does not prove that the compensating control itself was meaningfully tested unless scope, fault model, oracle, thresholds, and evidence freshness are fixed.
controls.counterexample_analysis: A compensating rate limiter links to a passing test that only checks the configuration file exists and never sends excess traffic. It is an executed result, so the clauses pass although effectiveness was not tested.

controls.reason: Mapping identifiers is mechanical, but selecting applicable security controls and deciding whether a verification standard is recognized and suitable requires security judgment.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every security control marked applicable in the approved scope record maps to a versioned control identifier in the selected standard.

controls.reason: Determining applicable privacy controls and their correspondence to legal and organizational requirements requires authorized privacy and legal interpretation.
Mapping identifiers to a selected WCAG version is checkable, but deciding applicable accessibility requirements and whether mappings are semantically correct requires specialist review.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every accessibility requirement approved as applicable maps to a criterion in the versioned selected WCAG conformance target.

controls.reason: Recorded links to operational requirements are checkable, but whether the selected SLO, incident, continuity, and recovery requirements are complete and appropriate is contextual.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every approved operational control references versioned SLO, incident, continuity, or recovery requirement records.

controls.reason: Contractual applicability and correct mapping across customer, processor, provider, and partner agreements require interpretation by authorized contract or legal specialists.
Finding conflicts across product, legal, and technical requirements requires semantic interpretation of an open-ended document set; absence of detected conflicts is not proof.
Resolution and approval fields can be checked for known conflict records, but the full set of actual conflicts and adequacy of each resolution require contextual or legal judgment.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every conflict in the approved conflict register has a resolution record, approving identity, authority evidence, and decision timestamp.

controls.reason: The proposal lacks a complete change inventory and makes high-impact classification an upstream authority decision; omitted or downgraded changes evade identity separation.
controls.counterexample_analysis: An administrator implements and self-approves a production data migration but labels it ordinary. Every record classified high-impact has different identities, so the clauses pass while a real high-impact change lacks separation.

controls.reason: Review cadence and signed review records are checkable, but deciding whether the selected control level still matches current application risk is an accountable judgment.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Control-level review records occur within the cadence required by the approved review policy and are bound to the current risk record.

controls.reason: Existence and revision timing of a system-context artifact are checkable, but whether it is accurate, complete, and truly up to date requires semantic comparison with the system.

deterministic_clauses.statement: A system-context diagram artifact exists and its revision is not older than the latest recorded architecture change.

controls.reason: Whether component and deployment diagrams are complete, accurate, and maintained cannot be established from file presence without interpreting actual topology.
End-to-end data-flow completeness requires discovering and interpreting every flow across code, infrastructure, operations, and external systems, an unbounded semantic claim.
Trust boundaries depend on identity, control, tenancy, and authority context; two informed reviewers may draw different valid boundaries from identical diagrams.
The proposal does not define authoritative network boundaries or prove a complete reachable-interface inventory across accounts, proxies, tunnels, and third parties.
controls.counterexample_analysis: A debug endpoint exposed through a forgotten load balancer is missing from environment evidence and unmarked in the architecture. Every discovered endpoint is marked, so the checker passes.

controls.reason: Classifying an interface as administrative or support-facing depends on intended use and privilege context that is not reliably inferable from endpoints alone.
Authentication and authorization decisions may be distributed through code, policy, infrastructure, and providers; proving every decision location is marked is unbounded and semantic.
Encryption and decryption boundaries span code, libraries, proxies, storage, clients, and providers, so complete marking cannot be proven from a bounded generic repository view.
Machine records can list known data operations, but sensitive-data classification and complete lifecycle-flow coverage require privacy expertise and semantic system understanding.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every sensitive-data operation in the approved data inventory has a lifecycle-stage marker in the structured data-flow record.

controls.reason: Identifying all third-party data transfers requires complete runtime, contractual, and data-flow knowledge plus privacy interpretation; absence in a diagram is not proof.
State can exist in application memory, files, databases, caches, queues, clients, and providers, so generic evidence cannot prove every stateful component was identified.
Asynchronous boundaries include explicit queues and hidden provider or callback behavior, making a complete generic inventory unsafe to infer from repository patterns.
Determining common dependencies and shared failure domains requires architecture and operational dependency reasoning beyond an exact graph-edge presence check.
A single point of failure depends on failure modes, redundancy behavior, traffic, and recovery assumptions; no required analysis or test protocol is defined.
Which control-plane dependencies are needed during varied incidents and recovery paths requires scenario-specific operational judgment and cannot be fully enumerated mechanically.
Cycles in a sealed dependency graph are deterministic, but hidden chains and completeness of that graph require contextual discovery, so the whole control is not deterministic.

deterministic_clauses.statement: A bounded graph traversal reports every cycle in the sealed declared dependency graph.

controls.reason: Choosing required consistency, ordering, durability, and freshness properties and acceptable thresholds is an architecture decision based on product consequences.
Determining which architectural invariants are necessary and whether the recorded set is complete requires expert design judgment rather than structural document validation.
Dependency-to-failure-record coverage can be checked, but criticality, relevant failure modes, and adequacy of expected behavior remain contextual architecture judgments.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every dependency marked critical in the approved inventory references a release-bound failure-behavior record.

controls.reason: Materiality and whether rejected alternatives are sufficiently recorded depend on design context; a decision-record file count cannot prove this control.
Known classified architecture changes can be compared with diagram revisions, but deciding whether every release change affects data flow, trust, topology, or dependencies is semantic.

deterministic_clauses.statement: For every change already classified as affecting architecture, all required diagram revisions are newer than the change record.

controls.reason: A structured component diff is possible, but verifying that documentation accurately represents all deployed architecture semantics requires a defined protocol and contextual interpretation.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every deployed component and connection in the authoritative environment snapshot has a corresponding identifier in the structured architecture record.

controls.reason: A release-bound threat-model record can prove that a review occurred, but whether it is a real and adequate threat model for the actual scope requires expert judgment.

deterministic_clauses.statement: A threat-model record exists and is bound to the assessed release identity and scope digest.

controls.reason: Completeness across all trust boundaries, actors, entry points, data stores, and external systems depends on complete architecture discovery and expert threat-model review.
A heading or scenario tagged spoofing does not prove identity attacks were meaningfully modeled; adequacy depends on system-specific threat analysis.
Determining whether unauthorized modification and integrity attacks were adequately modeled requires expert analysis of assets, boundaries, and plausible attack paths.
Information-disclosure and privacy attack modeling depends on sensitive-data context, affected people, legal duties, and specialist threat analysis.
Adequate denial-of-service and resource-exhaustion modeling depends on architecture, attacker capacity, quotas, and failure behavior rather than category-label presence.
Privilege-escalation modeling requires interpreting trust transitions, identities, permissions, and attack paths; a deterministic keyword check would be partial.
Repudiation and accountability threats depend on business actions, evidence needs, and trust boundaries, so model adequacy requires contextual security judgment.
Business-logic abuse is product-specific and open to varied attacker strategies; scenario presence cannot prove the relevant abuse was adequately modeled.
Insider and compromised-administrator threats depend on privileged workflows, organizational controls, and plausible misuse paths requiring expert interpretation.
Dependency and build-system compromise modeling requires supply-chain context and expert selection of credible attack paths, not just tool or document presence.
Tenant-escape and cross-customer attack applicability and adequacy depend on tenancy architecture, isolation boundaries, and specialist threat analysis.
Automation, scraping, spam, fraud, and economic abuse form an open-ended adversarial space whose complete and adequate modeling cannot be mechanically established.
Recovery-system and backup attacks depend on operational topology, credentials, retention, restore paths, and attacker models requiring contextual analysis.
Social-engineering threats in support and account recovery depend on human workflows, identity proofing, and attacker behavior that require expert review.
Threat-to-requirement and test links are checkable, but deciding whether each requirement and test actually addresses its threat requires semantic security review.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every identified threat record references at least one requirement and one test record that exist in the sealed evidence set.

controls.reason: Review timestamps for changes already labeled material are checkable, but deciding whether all design or scope changes are material requires contextual architecture judgment.

deterministic_clauses.statement: Every change recorded as material has a later threat-model review bound to the resulting release scope.

controls.reason: The check has no complete system inventory and depends on accountable high-value or high-risk classification; omitted or downgraded systems avoid review entirely.
controls.counterexample_analysis: A payment system is classified medium-risk and omitted from the applicable-system set, so it has no independent review. Every system marked high-risk has a signed review, and the proposal passes.
